# Event-Driven Architecture, Worked Out

Source: https://pasekpasek.github.io/event-driven-architecture-worked-out/
Author: Paweł Pasek
Verified against: a real node:http server (SSE parsing), an independent oracle port of 4th-devs'
scheduler (DAG readiness), the literal recovery.ts formula (backoff). Broker guarantees cited from
vendor docs.

A producer publishes a fact. Something, eventually, reacts to it. Everything else — brokers,
Server-Sent Events, streaming model output, multi-agent orchestration — is a variation on that one
relationship. This is the plain-text version of the page, without the sandboxes.

## 01. Three things always true

Most explanations of event-driven architecture open with a diagram: boxes for services, arrows for
messages, a cylinder for a queue. The diagram is a consequence. Start one level lower, with what
makes something "event-driven" rather than just "asynchronous."

1. A producer does not know who, if anyone, consumes an event it publishes. There is no return value
   and no caller identity — publishing is not the same operation as calling. Contrast a function
   call, where the caller knows exactly what it invoked and gets a value back. An event has none of
   that: zero, one, or a hundred consumers may react, and the producer's code is identical in every
   case.
2. An event describes a fact that has already happened — price.changed, not "change the price". A
   consumer that fails to process it does not un-happen it. This is why retrying a failed consumer is
   safe in a way retrying a failed RPC often isn't: the fact is still true, and processing it again
   should converge to the same result (see idempotency, §10).
3. Coupling doesn't disappear, it moves: from "who do I call" (a function reference, a service URL)
   to "what shape do I emit, what shape do I expect to read." A schema change is now the thing that
   breaks consumers, not a moved endpoint.

Most of what follows is one of these three facts wearing a costume: a Kafka partition is fact 1 with
a specific answer to "how many consumers, in what order"; an AI agent reacting to another agent's
completion is fact 2, with the agent as both producer and consumer.

One section is deliberately not. §06 is about Server-Sent Events, and SSE breaks fact 1: the server
holds one specific client's connection and writes straight down it, knowing exactly who is on the
other end. That is the opposite of a producer not knowing its consumers — which is precisely why it
is worth a section. Every event-driven system eventually has an edge where events stop being
broadcast to whoever cares and start being written to one identified reader. SSE is what that edge
looks like.

The page opens with a clickable dependency map: the three facts across the top, every later section
hanging off the one it derives from.

## 02. If you had to build it

An event needs something to hold it and something to eventually call the right reactions. Four
drafts, each fixing the last one's problem, arrive at the shape every real broker takes.

- Draft 1 — an in-process EventEmitter: `bus.on("price.changed", ...)` / `bus.emit(...)`.
  Synchronous, at-most-once, and the event never existed outside process memory: crash between emit
  and the listener finishing and it's simply gone. Fine within one process; not durable enough for
  anything that must survive a restart.
- Draft 2 — append to a durable log before dispatch: `appendFileSync("events.log", ...)` then emit.
  The fact survives a crash. But dispatch is still a one-shot in-memory broadcast: a consumer that
  starts five minutes later never sees it. Durability of the fact and delivery to a consumer are two
  different problems.
- Draft 3 — a reader tracks its own position: keep an `offset` into the log, slice from it, remember
  the new offset after processing. A restarted consumer can now resume from its own offset instead of
  the producer's broadcast moment. But if the process crashes after reading and before persisting the
  new offset, that event is redelivered. That's not a bug to fix — it's the origin of "at-least-once."
- Draft 4 — acknowledge or redeliver: give every delivered-but-unacknowledged event a deadline; if it
  isn't acknowledged in time, hand it out again. That one rule is a broker's visibility timeout (SQS),
  its consumer-group session timeout (Kafka) and its ack-wait (NATS JetStream) — three names for the
  same fix to the problem Draft 3 exposed.

Each draft fixes the previous one's gap: 1 reacts at all but can't survive a crash; 2 survives a
crash but can't reach a consumer that wasn't listening; 3 resumes after a restart but can't tell
"processed" from "crashed mid-process"; 4 redelivers what wasn't acknowledged but can't guarantee a
redelivery isn't processed twice (§10: idempotency).

## 03. Delivery guarantees, for real

"At-least-once" and "exactly-once" get repeated as marketing lines. Defined precisely:

- At-most-once — delivered zero or one times; a crash between send and receipt loses it silently.
- At-least-once — delivered one or more times; a crash between processing and acknowledging causes a
  redelivery. The consumer must tolerate duplicates.
- Exactly-once — the observed effect happens once, even if the underlying delivery is at-least-once
  underneath (achieved via deduplication or idempotent writes, not by magically never redelivering).

What four real systems document:

- Kafka: at-least-once. Exactly-once needs an idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true) and a
  transactional consumer (isolation.level=read_committed). Ordering: within one partition only (§04).
- SQS standard: at-least-once, best-effort — duplicates and reordering both possible. No ordering.
- SQS FIFO: exactly-once processing via deduplication. Ordering within one Message Group ID only.
- SNS standard: at-least-once per subscriber. No ordering across the fanout.
- SNS FIFO: exactly-once, SQS FIFO subscribers only. Ordering within one message group.
- EventBridge: at-least-once, automatic retry, per-rule DLQ. No ordering.

None of these are run locally on this page — there's no browser-executable "real Kafka" to diff
against, the way libuv could be diffed for the event loop page. These rows are quoted from the
vendors' own documentation, not independently reproduced.

## 04. Ordering, partitioning and parallelism

"The event happened first" and "a consumer sees it first" are different claims. Nothing connects them
unless a specific mechanism does.

Kafka orders messages only within a partition. A topic's messages across partitions have no defined
relative order at all. A producer picks the partition via a key — same key, same partition, so events
for that key are ordered relative to each other, but two different keys give no guarantee either way.
SQS FIFO does the equivalent with a Message Group ID instead of a partition key: order is preserved
only within one group.

Ordering is what partitions constrain; it is not what they are for. A partition is the unit of
parallelism. Kafka's introduction: a topic is "spread over a number of 'buckets' located on
different Kafka brokers," and that placement "is very important for scalability because it allows
client applications to both read and write the data from/to many brokers at the same time." Within
a consumer group each partition goes to at most one consumer, so the partition count is the ceiling
on consumer parallelism. Therefore ordering and throughput are bought with the same currency:
picking a partition key is picking how small a scope you are willing to keep ordered (per customer,
per SKU) so everything outside that scope runs in parallel. "Order events globally" is not a
requirement anyone can fill; "order events per customer" is a key.

Two patterns hide behind the word "consumer". Competing consumers: exactly one member of a group
gets the event (SQS deletes it after a successful receive; a Kafka group hands each partition to one
member) — this shares work, and adding a worker changes nothing semantically. Fan-out: every
subscriber gets its own copy and its own position (SNS subscribers, or separate Kafka consumer
groups on one topic) — this adds behaviour, and the producer still doesn't know (fact 1). One Kafka
topic does both: consumers within a group compete, groups between themselves fan out. Two teams
reading one topic without noticing they share a group will each process half the events, and it
looks exactly like random data loss.

The page's sandbox emits events for two keys (sku-1, sku-2) into two partitions, each consumed by
its own worker, and shows the combined "topic order" a consumer sees: each key's own events stay
ordered relative to each other, but the two sequences interleave arbitrarily — and in single-key
mode the second worker has nothing to do, which is the throughput half of the trade made visible.

Source: Apache Kafka — Introduction (https://kafka.apache.org/intro).

## 05. What goes in an event, and what breaks when it changes

Fact 3 said coupling moves into the shape of the event. That is two decisions per event type: what
goes inside it, and what happens the day it changes.

Three shapes, in Martin Fowler's terminology
(https://martinfowler.com/articles/201701-event-driven.html):

- Event notification — the event carries {"orderId":"o-1042"} and nothing else. Every consumer must
  call back for details, which re-introduces exactly the runtime coupling fact 1 removed, and the
  callback reads current state, which may already have moved past the event being reacted to.
- Event-carried state transfer — the event carries the fields consumers need. No callback; an
  offline consumer can catch up without talking to the producer. In exchange every field is a
  published promise. This is the default worth reaching for.
- Event sourcing — every change kept forever, state is the fold over the log (§09). The log is the
  database, with everything that implies.

Schema evolution, with Confluent Schema Registry's vocabulary
(https://docs.confluent.io/platform/current/schema-registry/fundamentals/schema-evolution.html):
BACKWARD compatibility (the default) "means that consumers using the new schema can read data
produced with the last schema"; FORWARD means "data produced with a new schema can be read by
consumers using the last schema." Adding or removing an optional field is allowed under both; that
is the entire safe set. For JSON Schema, compatibility "depends on both the compatibility policy and
the content model (additionalProperties: true for open, false for closed)" — so whether adding a
field is safe is a fact about your consumers, not about your event.

Practical rules: add, don't change; never rename in place (a rename is a delete plus an add, and it
breaks every reader of the old name at once); never retype in place (this one fails silently); a
genuinely breaking change becomes a new event type published alongside the old until the old goes
quiet, with the version in the type name (order.placed.v2), because fact 1 means you cannot
enumerate who to warn.

The page's sandbox publishes {"type":"order.placed","orderId":"o-1042","total":4999} to three
consumers — a tolerant reader, a strict validator with additionalProperties:false, and a billing
consumer that sums totals — and applies one change at a time. Adding a field: tolerant ok, validator
rejects, billing ok. Renaming total: all three break. Retyping total to the string "49.99": the
validator rejects, and the other two keep running and produce "049.99" by string concatenation — the
silent failure. Publishing a v2 alongside v1: nobody breaks. The full 5 × 3 matrix is asserted by
test-model.ts.

## 06. What SSE actually is, and what it isn't

Server-Sent Events is not event-driven architecture. It is a transport — one connection, one
identified reader, no broker, no fan-out, no durability. Its place in this page is the seam: it is
where an event-driven system stops talking to itself and starts writing to somebody.

First, the part that really is event-driven. Inside a process, fact 1 is cheap to satisfy. The whole
event bus 4th-devs runs its agent system on (05_01_agent_graph/src/events.ts) is a sequence counter,
a Set of listeners and a bounded buffer: `emit` pushes the event into the buffer and calls every
listener without knowing or caring who they are; `subscribe` adds one and hands back an unsubscribe;
`replay()` returns the buffer so a listener that attaches late still gets everything that already
happened. That is §02's Draft 1 and Draft 2 in about forty lines, and it never leaves the process.

Then, the wire. The events have to reach a dashboard in a browser: one specific reader, across a
process boundary, over HTTP. That is SSE — one HTTP response that never ends. No upgrade handshake, no new protocol — just
Content-Type: text/event-stream on an ordinary response the server keeps writing to, and a client
that knows how to read it as a sequence of events instead of one blob. One direction only: server to
client. A client that wants to talk back makes a separate, ordinary HTTP request.

The body is lines of `field: value`. A blank line means "dispatch what's buffered so far":

    id: 42
    event: task.completed
    data: {"taskId":"write-intro","actor":"writer"}

    data: a plain message with no id or type — dispatched as "message"

- data: — the payload. Multiple data: lines before a blank line are joined with newlines into one event.
- event: — the event type a client can filter on with addEventListener(type, ...); omitted, it
  dispatches as the generic "message" event.
- id: — the reconnect checkpoint. The browser remembers the last one it saw and resends it as a
  Last-Event-ID request header if the connection drops and it reconnects.
- retry: — how many milliseconds to wait before that automatic reconnect.

A minimal SSE server is a handful of lines, quoted unmodified from 4th-devs
(05_01_agent_graph/src/server.ts, sseHandler): write the text/event-stream headers, flush them, write
every buffered past event as `data: ...\n\n`, then subscribe and write each new event the same way.

That adapter is the whole trick, and it is why "is SSE event-driven?" is the wrong question. The bus
is event-driven; the socket is not; `subscribe(event => res.write(...))` is the bridge between them.
Swap the right-hand side for a Kafka producer and the left-hand side does not change — which is what
fact 3 predicted: the coupling that survives is the shape of the event, not who reads it.

Notice it replays every buffered past event on every new connection, unconditionally — it never reads
a Last-Event-ID header at all. That's a legitimate, simpler design for a small bounded buffer: the
client re-renders from scratch and de-duplicates by id, so exact resumption doesn't need to be the
server's job. The client side is equally small: `const es = new EventSource("/events");` plus an
onmessage handler.

## 07. AI model streaming as an SSE application

"The model streams its response" is section 5, with a schema. Set stream: true on an Anthropic
Messages API call and the response is exactly a text/event-stream, readable by the same
EventSource-shaped logic — only now the event types and payloads are documented, not ad hoc.

One turn is a fixed sequence: message_start (the message shell, with an empty content array), then
per content block content_block_start → repeated content_block_delta → content_block_stop, then
message_delta (carrying the final stop_reason) and message_stop. A ping event may appear between
deltas purely as a keep-alive, with no content of its own — the same role as the `: connected` comment
line a raw SSE server can send.

A tool call is a content block whose content_block_start has "type": "tool_use" and a partial,
growing set of arguments: each content_block_delta for that block carries an input_json_delta with a
partial_json string fragment, not a complete value. The fragments must be concatenated and are only
guaranteed parseable once content_block_stop closes the block — the exact same "buffer until the
boundary" rule as an SSE data: field in §06, one level up the stack.

The page's stepper walks a real tool-use turn quoted verbatim from Anthropic's own streaming
documentation, showing the tool input accumulating as an incomplete JSON string
({"location": → "San → Francisc → o, → CA"}) until the block closes and it parses.

## 08. Agents as event-driven systems

An agent's "loop" — plan, act, observe, replan — is a consumer reacting to events: its own tool
result, another agent's completion, a human answering a question it posed. Wire several agents
together and the whole system is a graph of tasks reacting to each other's done events.

4th-devs implements this as a DAG: each task lists what it dependsOn; every round, the scheduler
recomputes the ready set — tasks whose dependencies are all done — and only those run. Its round loop
is the agent-world analogue of the event loop's phases:

1. Emit heartbeat.started.
2. Reconcile dependency blocks/unblocks.
3. Resolve waiting-on-a-human tasks.
4. Each agent claims one open task, runs it, the status transition is emitted as an event.
5. Emit heartbeat.idle if nothing was claimable, or mark the project done.
6. Emit heartbeat.finished; persist a snapshot of the round.

Where the graph comes from: nobody draws it. It is built at runtime by agents calling a tool, and
that tool call is the one from §07 — the arguments that arrived as partial_json fragments and only
became parseable when the content block closed. The tool is delegate_task
(https://github.com/i-am-alice/4th-devs/blob/main/05_01_agent_graph/src/tools/task/delegate.ts),
whose dependsOnTaskIds parameter is described as "Task ids that must finish before this task can
run", and whose handler contains the single line that creates the edge:

    status: dependsOnTaskIds.length > 0 ? 'waiting' : 'todo',

So the chain runs end to end: a model emits input_json_delta fragments over SSE (§07); they
concatenate into the arguments to delegate_task; the handler writes a task whose dependsOn is the
edge; the scheduler walks the graph the model just drew. The ready set is not a diagram — it is
whatever the agents have talked themselves into so far.

The same file is the clearest example of fact 2 on the page. delegate_task and complete_task are
commands: imperative, addressed to a handler, allowed to fail, awaited by the caller. What the
scheduler emits afterwards — task.completed, task.blocked — are events: past tense, addressed to
nobody, not refusable. Mixing the two up produces topics full of names like send.email, which read
as instructions and make the producer responsible for whoever was meant to obey them.

The page's sandbox runs the exact findReadyTasks/runRound functions that test-model.ts verifies
against an independently written oracle (ported from
https://github.com/i-am-alice/4th-devs/blob/main/05_01_agent_graph/src/scheduler/graph.ts and
loop.ts), over a five-task graph: fetch-price and fetch-inventory have no dependencies; price-check
depends on both and also waits on its child sanity-check; notify depends on price-check. The
verification includes the case where sanity-check comes back blocked: a blocked child counts as
finished for its parent, so price-check and notify still complete.

## 09. Event sourcing and agent state

Nothing so far has stored "the current state" anywhere. It's derived: replay the event log from
empty, and you have it. That's not an implementation detail — it's a deliberate trade of storage
simplicity for compute-on-read.

4th-devs writes exactly this: an append-only events.jsonl, one JSON object per line, never edited,
only appended to (03_02_events/docs/schemas.md).

Two things fall out for free. Crash recovery: restart, replay the log, and the in-memory state is
exactly what it was — there is no separate "did the state file get corrupted" failure mode, because
there never was a state file, only the log. Observability: any question about "what happened, and
when" is answerable by reading the log, not by having remembered to instrument that specific question
in advance.

It doesn't stay free. A log that only ever grows eventually costs more to replay than a snapshot
would cost to load — which is exactly why Kafka ships log compaction (keeping only the latest record
per key) as a first-class feature, not an afterthought. Snapshotting is named here, not built: out of
scope for this page (§13).

## 10. Failure, retries, poison messages

Every "at-least-once" system in §03 can redeliver. That's not a bug the consumer waits out — it's a
contract the consumer must be written for: processing the same event twice has to converge to the
same result (idempotency), or duplicates corrupt state.

The real backoff formula, verified by test-model.ts against 4th-devs' recovery.ts:

    const delay = Math.min(15_000, 1_500 * 2 ** (attempt - 1));
    // attempt 1: 1500ms  2: 3000ms  3: 6000ms  4: 12000ms  5+: 15000ms (capped)

A message that keeps failing past a limit — 4th-devs caps auto-retry at 3 attempts — is a poison
message: something is genuinely wrong with it, not just transiently unlucky, and retrying forever
would starve everything behind it. Real brokers name this explicitly: SQS's redrive policy moves a
message to a dead-letter queue after a configured maxReceiveCount; Kafka has no built-in DLQ, so the
convention is application-level — publish the poison message to a separate <topic>.DLT topic instead
of committing its offset normally.

The formula has no jitter, and most production backoffs do. Every consumer knocked over by the same
outage computes the same delay from the same formula and comes back at the same instant, knocking
the recovering service down again — a thundering herd on a schedule. The fix is to sleep a random
duration up to the computed ceiling. The page quotes 4th-devs' jitter-free formula and names jitter
as a production change rather than attributing it.

Idempotency, concretely: processing the same event twice leaves the system in the same state as
processing it once. Three ways there, in ascending order of bookkeeping:

    // 1. Not idempotent. A redelivery double-counts — silently, permanently, as real money.
    UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + $1 WHERE id = $2

    // 2. Naturally idempotent: the event says what the world IS, not how much it moved.
    UPDATE accounts SET balance = $1 WHERE id = $2

    // 3. Made idempotent with the event's own id, in ONE transaction with the effect.
    INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
    -- if no row was inserted, return; otherwise apply the effect, same transaction

Option 2 is not a consumer fix at all — it is the §05 decision made well. An event carrying a delta
forces every consumer to be exactly-once or be wrong; an event carrying the resulting state lets a
consumer be sloppy and still land correct, so one field in the payload can buy idempotency for the
whole downstream.

Two things about option 3: the transaction is not decoration (put the dedup insert in a different
transaction from the effect, or in Redis, and you have rebuilt the dual write of §11, with a new
failure where the marker says "handled" and the work never happened); and processed_events grows
forever, so you prune it by age, which makes deduplication exactly as good as that retention window.
SQS FIFO has the same limit and says so: "within a 5-minute deduplication window, only one instance
of a message with the same deduplication ID is processed and delivered"
(https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/using-messagededuplicationid-property.html).

The page's sandbox delivers evt-1 (+500) and evt-2 (+300) under the three designs and lets you
redeliver evt-1. Under "balance += amount" the redelivery reaches 1000. Under the absolute write it
stays 500. Under dedup it is ignored. The last run matters most: deliver evt-1, deliver evt-2, then
redeliver evt-1 under the absolute write, and the balance walks backwards to 500 — the write was
idempotent and still wrong, because idempotent is not order-proof. That needs a version guard
(UPDATE ... WHERE version < :v), which is §04 arriving in the consumer. All of it is asserted by
test-model.ts.

## 11. The dual write: outbox and CDC

Every example on this page has quietly cheated. Each one writes something down and publishes an event
about it, and assumes both happen. They cannot — not atomically. A database transaction does not
extend to Kafka, and the process can die in the gap. Write first and publish second: the process dies
in between and the order exists while nobody was told. Publish first and write second: you have
announced a fact that is not true yet. No ordering of the two calls fixes it, because the problem is
not the order — it is that two separate systems cannot agree without a transaction spanning both.

The outbox: stop doing two writes. In the same local transaction that stores the order, insert a row
into an `outbox` table describing the event. One transaction, one system, atomic. A separate relay
reads unpublished outbox rows, pushes them to the broker and marks them sent. The crash does not
disappear, it becomes survivable: die before the relay runs and the row is still there on restart;
die after publishing but before marking it sent and the relay publishes twice — at-least-once again
(§03), which is why the consumer must be idempotent (§10). The outbox does not buy exactly-once; it
buys "never silently lost".

CDC answers the same question from the other side: instead of writing an event by hand, read the
database's own replication log (Postgres' WAL, MySQL's binlog) and turn each committed row change
into an event. The write is the event, so there is nothing to keep in sync. Debezium is the usual
implementation. The trade is fact 3 collected: with an outbox you choose the event's shape; with CDC
the shape is whatever your table looks like, so a column rename breaks every consumer — the schema
stops being an internal detail and becomes the public contract.

The page's sandbox lets you tick "crash", place an order and compare the modes: direct dual write
loses the event permanently, outbox mode leaves a pending row the relay still publishes.

## 12. What you give up

Everything before this is mechanism, and mechanism reads like advocacy. The bill, paid on day one
whether or not the decoupling ever pays you back:

- The call stack is gone. "Why did this happen" used to be answerable by reading downwards. The
  causal chain is now spread across processes and time, and nothing reconstructs it unless you built
  that: a correlation id threaded through every event and log line, or a tracing system. Teams
  discover this during an incident, which is the worst moment to start adding correlation ids.
- "Find all callers" stops working. There are no callees behind emit('order.placed'); the new call
  graph is grepping for a string literal, and it misses dynamic subscriptions and names built by
  concatenation. Fact 1 is a runtime property you wanted and a static-analysis property you gave up.
- Eventual consistency becomes somebody's UX problem. The user clicks save and the list is
  maintained by a consumer that hasn't run yet. Spinner, optimistic update, or stale data — there is
  no fourth option, and the choice belongs to whoever designs the screen.
- Testing moves to the seams. Every service's unit tests can pass while the system is broken,
  because the failure is a field one team renamed (§05) and another read. Contract tests catch it,
  and they are written after the first incident rather than before.
- You operate a broker: upgrades, disk pressure, partition sizing (§04), consumer-lag alerting, and
  somebody whose actual job is to read the dead-letter queue. An unread DLQ is a data-loss bug that
  files itself neatly and waits.

When not to: one service, one database, one consumer you own and deploy together — write the
function call. The bet pays only when you hold what it buys: consumers you don't control, can't
enumerate, or that must survive your downtime, or one fact with several genuinely independent
reactions. If you can name your consumer, you don't have that yet. Events are a wager that not
knowing your consumers gains you more than not knowing your consumers costs you; frequently a good
wager, never a free one.

The page's sandbox shows ten log lines from four services for two interleaved orders, and asks which
order got the "payment problem" email and why. Without a correlation id the question is unanswerable
from true, complete logs; with one it takes a click. Same incident, same services, same logs — the
difference is one field somebody either threaded through beforehand or didn't.

## 13. The whole page in rules, and scope

1. A producer doesn't know its consumers; an event is a fact, not a request — a failed consumer
   doesn't un-happen it.
2. "At-least-once" is the practical default everywhere (Kafka, SQS standard, EventBridge);
   exactly-once is achieved on top of it via idempotency or dedup, not by avoiding redelivery.
3. Ordering is scoped: to a Kafka partition, to an SQS Message Group ID — never to a whole topic or
   queue. A partition is also the unit of parallelism, so ordering and throughput are bought with
   the same currency: picking a key is picking how small a scope you keep ordered.
4. Consumers within one group compete for events; separate groups each get their own copy. The same
   topic does both, and confusing them looks exactly like random data loss.
5. Prefer an event that says what the world now is over one that says how much it moved: it makes
   every downstream consumer idempotent for free. Adding an optional field is the only safe change;
   a rename breaks everyone at once, a type change breaks them silently; a genuinely breaking change
   is a new event type published beside the old one, because fact 1 means you cannot enumerate who
   to warn.
6. SSE is one HTTP response the server keeps writing to, in the wire format data:/event:/id:/retry:,
   one direction only.
7. AI model streaming is SSE with a documented event schema: message_start → per-block
   content_block_start/delta/stop → message_delta → message_stop. Tool-call arguments arrive as JSON
   fragments that are only safe to parse once their block closes.
8. A multi-agent system is a DAG reacting to done events; the ready set is recomputed every round,
   the same shape as an event loop's phases one level up.
9. Agent state doesn't have to be stored directly — folding an append-only event log recovers it, for
   free, until the log itself needs compaction.
10. A consumer under at-least-once delivery must be idempotent; a message that keeps failing past a
   limit belongs in a dead-letter queue, not in an infinite retry loop.
11. You cannot write to a database and publish an event atomically. Make it one local write — an
   outbox row in the same transaction, or the replication log itself (CDC) — and let a relay publish,
   or accept that a crash in the gap loses the event silently. The same rule governs a deduplication
   table: mark the event handled in the same transaction as the effect, or you have built the dual
   write again.
12. The bill arrives on day one: no stack trace, no "find all callers", eventual consistency visible
   on someone's screen, and a broker to operate. If you can name your one consumer, write the
   function call instead.

Left out, on purpose. The outbox and change-data-capture have a section of their own (§11). Two more
a production system hits early, named rather than half-explained:

- Sagas. Once a workflow spans services there is no transaction to roll back. A saga replaces
  rollback with explicit compensating actions — refund the payment, release the reservation — which
  means designing the undo for every step, and accepting that the system is briefly, visibly
  inconsistent while it runs.
- End-to-end exactly-once. §03's exactly-once claims stop at each broker's own boundary. Chaining two
  systems together does not compose their guarantees; the joint is where duplicates reappear, and
  idempotency (§10) is the only thing that actually travels.

## About this page's models

Five of this page's models are backed by running code, checked by test-model.ts (21 checks):

- The SSE parser is checked against a real node:http server, including an event deliberately split
  across two TCP-level writes, over a real fetch + ReadableStream client.
- The DAG scheduler (ready-set computation, parent-unblocking, and the case where a child comes back
  blocked and still has to unblock its parent) is checked against an independently-written oracle
  port of the real algorithm in 4th-devs (05_01_agent_graph/src/scheduler/graph.ts and loop.ts) —
  two separate implementations of the same real logic, not one copy-pasted into the other.
- The backoff formula is checked against the literal formula in 4th-devs
  (05_01_agent_graph/src/scheduler/recovery.ts, computeRetryDelayMs).
- The §05 schema-evolution matrix is asserted verdict by verdict across five changes and three
  consumers, so the claim that a retype fails silently for two of them is executed, not described.
- The §10 idempotency models are checked: delta reaches 1000 after a redelivery, the absolute write
  stays 500, dedup ignores the duplicate, and the out-of-order absolute write is idempotent and
  still wrong.

Everything about Kafka, SQS, SNS, EventBridge and NATS delivery/ordering guarantees is not modeled —
those systems aren't run locally; those claims are cited and quoted from official documentation, as
are Confluent's schema-compatibility definitions and Fowler's event-shape taxonomy. The
§07 streaming fixture is quoted verbatim from Anthropic's own published documentation, not captured
from a live API call.

Run the harness: node test-model.ts
